cim: Opinion: Finding hope in artificial intelligence
cim_eredeti: Opinion: Finding hope in artificial intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
“Optimism is a passive virtue; hope is an active one.” — Rabbi Jonathan Sacks

With the onslaught of artificial intelligence comes a seemingly endless series of stories that market doom and gloom: how we are losing our touch with humanity, the ethical and moral backsliding from tech CEOs, and AI bots taking on a life of their own.

While we all should remain critical of the “inevitable” arrival of tools that threaten human life and human dignity, there is more to this wave of technology than the end of humankind. In fact, our ability to see artificial intelligence as an opportunity is essential to our ability to harness its power for good.

A few months ago, I sat in a room of “peacetech” founders, an emerging technology sector created in deliberate defiance of defense tech, unified around the mission of using technology, including artificial intelligence for peace. The term peacetech is attributed to several sources including the PeaceTech Lab launched in partnership with the United States Institute for Peace in 2008, and is defined as “the movement to use technology to end violence and extremism.”

Founder after founder presented their pitch, with clarity around how artificial intelligence can create a world of greater collaboration and peace. Products included everything from new software to amplify distribution of humanitarian aid to genocide prevention, and after each pitch, the room — packed with venture capital firms, independent investors, partners, nonprofits and government officials — would erupt into applause.

Peacetech is more than just “AI for good” or the idea around ease of living. Centered as the focus of the recent U.N. summit, AI for Good showcases how AI can improve everyday life but isn’t necessarily centered on ending conflict. Peacetech is the deliberate tool we need for peace, strengthening democracy, ensuring free and fair elections, and helping to put better tools in the hands of those working to prevent conflict.

I have no optimism for AI, nor its ability, in the hands of technology companies to instinctively choose what’s best for humanity, but I have hope that we can harness AI to do more good, at scale, than previously known.

One such company is using AI and WhatsApp to tutor thousands of students in Africa. Another is supporting mental health for veterans by testing the limits of chatbot responses. For each case study of AI missteps, we can provide stories of peacetech and challenge corporations and universities to become the platform for competition to innovate for peace.

One tangible way to participate in the peacetech movement is to be deliberate in the way you share information with artificial intelligence. AI can use everything from private conversations over text, social media posts and cookies online to create mass surveillance that threatens peace.

Meredith Whittaker, the CEO of Signal, has created an alternative mass communication app that prioritizes user privacy, and now has 70 million users after WhatsApp disclosed to users that it would share private data to Facebook and its affiliates. Signal is being used by democracy freedom fighters so that private communications can’t be weaponized by authoritarian governments. Signal is used to prevent emerging AI surveillance. Changing the narrative on peacetech is informed by how we share our information online.

AI gives us an opportunity to think about technology in new ways. Religious leaders recently met with Anthropic to encourage a code of ethics, but religious leaders can engage more directly with emerging peacetech — what if religious leaders were building tools to better serve the community? Feeding only one side of the narrative that generates fear, overwhelm and apathy is a disservice to humanity. It enables larger divides in society, including by age, income and sector.

Peacetech offers a model and solution to killer robots and technology divides. It demonstrates that hope is not something we wish for the future but that we build in the present. Rabbi Jonathan Sacks shared, “Optimism and hope are not the same. Optimism is the belief that the world is changing for the better; hope is the belief that, together, we can make the world better. Optimism is a passive virtue, hope an active one.” We need to counter the forces that are driving more to harness artificial intelligence for war and conflict and instead incentivize innovators, entrepreneurs, students, religious leaders and government to invest in and expand the influence of peacetech.

I have no optimism for AI, nor its ability, in the hands of technology companies to instinctively choose what’s best for humanity, but I have hope that we can harness AI to do more good, at scale, than previously known. If we are engaged and informed, if we rightly characterize AI as a machine and not as a conscious being, we can utilize AI as a tool to build more peacetech and ultimately more peace. I am committed to a world of hope and a world of new peacetech.
